why: Absolute military size captures the coercive capacity of the state; rapid expansions or contractions signal rearmament, coup-preparedness, or fiscal strain that precede political ruptures. It provides a raw-power baseline that complements spending-ratio indicators already in the pool.
coverage_note: WB WDI sourced from IISS; reasonable coverage from 1985 onward, thinner for small states and fragile states pre-1990.

trends.reason: Military size trajectory is a first-order predictor of coup feasibility; large, growing armies correlate with coup attempts.
Military mobilisation patterns directly precede interstate conflict escalation and are a structural readiness signal.
Force size relative to population captures counterinsurgency capacity and predicts conflict duration.
Step changes in personnel levels often coincide with formal military reform events.

why: Storm-related displacement isolates extreme-weather shock intensity from other hazard types, offering a cleaner signal of cyclone/typhoon exposure that degrades food security, displaces populations, and strains governance before broader humanitarian crises crystallise. Disaggregating by hazard type prevents flood and storm dynamics from cancelling each other out.
coverage_note: IDMC disaster disaggregated series starts 2008; storm events concentrated in tropical-cyclone-belt countries, many landlocked states show zero or near-zero rows.

trends.reason: Direct hazard-specific signal; storm displacement is the most salient feature for cyclone/flood event prediction.
Large storm displacement events are among the fastest pathways to acute humanitarian crises.
Repeated storm displacement cycles convert internal displacement into cross-border migration pressure.
Storm/cyclone displacement sometimes damages crops and storage, creating localized food insecurity as a secondary pathway.

why: This binary flags years when the state itself is the perpetrator of one-sided civilian killings, distinguishing regime-directed repression from battlefield violence — a critical distinction for predicting political crises, mass protest, and international intervention triggers. Its presence in a country-year sharply elevates the base rate of subsequent political ruptures.
coverage_note: UCDP one-sided violence dataset from 1989; only conflict-affected or repressive contexts contribute positives — large share of zeros for peaceful states is structurally meaningful.

trends.reason: Government-perpetrated killing is the definitional core event for political repression trends; near-certain top-feature candidate.
State-directed civilian deaths are among the most severe human rights violation signals in the pool.
State killing of civilians is a documented trigger for subsequent mass protest mobilisation.
International responses to atrocities (R2P invocations, no-fly zones) are preceded by government one-sided violence.

why: Diagonal accountability captures the watchdog power of civil society and independent media to hold executives to account — a dimension orthogonal to formal institutional checks, and one that erodes measurably before autocratisation accelerates. Declining diagonal accountability predicts democratic backsliding and repression events with a multi-year lead.
coverage_note: V-Dem covers virtually all countries from 1900; pre-1945 estimates carry higher coding uncertainty.

trends.reason: Diagonal accountability erosion is a canonical leading indicator of executive power grabs documented across autocratisation episodes.
Repressive states systematically weaken civil society and media before and during repression campaigns.
Diagonal accountability levels distinguish genuine democratisation from facade transitions.
Media and civil society constraints reduce anti-corruption oversight, correlating with corruption event escalation.

why: Independent trade union engagement measures the organisational infrastructure of civil society outside formal political channels; suppression of unions is an early governance stress indicator that also proxies for the social mobilisation capacity underpinning labour actions and mass protests. It captures a dimension of political competition not fully reflected in electoral indicators.
coverage_note: V-Dem full panel; coverage strongest post-1945; pre-1945 labour context harder to code for some regions.

trends.reason: Trade union organisational freedom directly determines the capacity and frequency of strike and labour action events.
Strong independent unions provide logistical backbone for mass protest coalitions beyond purely labour grievances.
Crackdowns on unions often accompany broader repression campaigns; union suppression is a repression leading indicator.
Organised labour pressure shapes social policy bargaining; union strength is a partial predictor of reform momentum.

why: Extractive state capacity — the government's ability to raise sustained revenues — is a foundational determinant of fiscal resilience, public goods provision, and regime stability; states that cannot tax reliably are far more vulnerable to fiscal crises, foreign-debt spirals, and popular delegitimisation. It is theoretically distinct from administrative or coercive capacity and adds non-redundant signal.
coverage_note: Hanson & Sigman dataset ends at 2015; post-2015 gap limits near-term predictive window unless complemented by WB tax-revenue indicators.

trends.reason: Revenue-raising capacity sets the structural ceiling for fiscal policy; low extractive capacity predicts austerity-forced policy shifts.
Governments with weak extractive capacity cannot backstop financial systems, raising sovereign-bank nexus vulnerability.
Low fiscal capacity limits counter-cyclical response, deepening and lengthening recessions.
Revenue-starved states sometimes resort to coercive rent extraction in lieu of legitimate taxation.

why: Total natural resource rents as a share of GDP measures the degree to which a state's economy and fiscal system depend on extractable resource windfalls — a key driver of Dutch disease, elite rent-seeking, and regime vulnerability to commodity price shocks. Resource-dependent states show systematically different instability pathways (boom-bust, coup risk, secessionism over resource zones).
coverage_note: WB WDI broad coverage from 1970; some micro-states and recent entrants have gaps; rents methodology revised several times so early series may not be fully comparable.

trends.reason: High resource rent dependency is the primary structural precondition for resource-driven conflict; near-definitive feature for this trend.
Total rents (majority oil/gas in most high-dependency states) directly tracks fiscal exposure driving oil-and-gas political events.
Nationalisation events cluster around resource-rich countries when rents shift or external prices spike.
Resource rent dependency increases conflict attractiveness via lootable wealth, funding rebel movements and prolonging wars.

why: Legislative oversight of the executive is a direct measure of institutional checks on executive power; its erosion is a near-universal precursor to authoritarian consolidation, corruption escalation, and constitutional crises. This indicator adds a horizontal accountability dimension distinct from judicial independence and civil society watchdog indicators.
coverage_note: V-Dem full panel; single-party or zero-legislature periods coded at floor values; coding reliability strongest post-1950.

trends.reason: Declining legislative oversight is a textbook step in executive power consolidation; high theoretical and empirical basis.
Constitutional changes that alter power balances are often preceded and enabled by weakened legislative oversight.
Weak oversight removes the primary institutional brake on executive corruption.
Dysfunctional legislatures create political vacuums that military actors exploit for coup justification.

why: Population-normalised conflict displacement provides a cross-country comparable intensity metric that raw displacement counts cannot: a country displacing 100,000 people out of 500,000 is qualitatively different from one displacing 100,000 out of 50 million. This normalised form is the ML-preferred input, reducing spurious country-size correlations in the greedy feature selection.
coverage_note: IDMC conflict displacement series starts 2009; countries with no recorded conflict show zero rows — structurally meaningful; sparse for very small island states.

trends.reason: Population-scale conflict displacement is a direct intensity proxy for active civil war and insurgency, likely to enter top features.
Normalised displacement captures humanitarian burden relative to country capacity, a core crisis severity signal.
High per-capita internal displacement is a strong predictor of subsequent cross-border refugee flows.
Conflict displacement at population scale reflects sustained political violence rather than isolated incidents.

why: Government-run domestic disinformation campaigns are a measurable indicator of information-environment weaponisation — a modern governance failure that undermines electoral integrity, suppresses opposition, and precedes democratic backsliding. As a V-Dem-coded indicator it is available at country-year resolution from 1990 onward, filling a gap not covered by traditional institutional indicators.
coverage_note: V-Dem social media indicators coded from 1990; pre-social-media years reflect offline propaganda proxies so early values require interpretation caution.

trends.reason: State disinformation is a signature tool of executive power consolidation, documented systematically in autocratisation literature.
Government disinformation campaigns peak around elections to suppress opposition and manipulate voter behaviour.
Information repression co-occurs with physical repression as complementary tools of political control.
Intensified disinformation can both suppress and — when publics detect manipulation — trigger reactive protest mobilisation.
